<a href="/wiki/File:Gary_Hart_and_Stephen_King,_1984_presidential_campaign.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Gary_Hart_and_Stephen_King%2C_1984_presidential_campaign.jpg/250px-Gary_Hart_and_Stephen_King%2C_1984_presidential_campaign.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="3198" data-file-width="4604" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/Gary_Hart_and_Stephen_King%2C_1984_presidential_campaign.jpg/500px-Gary_Hart_and_Stephen_King%2C_1984_presidential_campaign.jpg 2x" width="250" height="174" /></a>
<figcaption>King campaigning for <a href="/wiki/Gary_Hart" title="Gary Hart">Gary Hart</a> in 1984</figcaption>
</figure>

King was raised [Methodist](/wiki/Methodist "Methodist"){.mw-redirect},^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}150[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-150)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}151[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-OfficialFAQ-151)^ but lost his belief in organized religion while in high school. While not conventionally religious, he says he does believe in God.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}152[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-guardian-152)^

<figure class="mw-default-size mw-halign-right" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Dark,_chilling_night_in_Germany_with_Stephen_King_131118-F-YC884-226.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Dark%2C_chilling_night_in_Germany_with_Stephen_King_131118-F-YC884-226.jpg/250px-Dark%2C_chilling_night_in_Germany_with_Stephen_King_131118-F-YC884-226.jpg" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" data-file-height="2070" data-file-width="1154" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/66/Dark%2C_chilling_night_in_Germany_with_Stephen_King_131118-F-YC884-226.jpg/500px-Dark%2C_chilling_night_in_Germany_with_Stephen_King_131118-F-YC884-226.jpg 2x" width="190" height="341" /></a>
<figcaption>King at the <a href="/wiki/Ramstein_Air_Base" title="Ramstein Air Base">Ramstein Air Base</a> in Germany, 2013</figcaption>
</figure>

King has supported several Democrats in presidential races. In [1984](/wiki/1984_United_States_presidential_election "1984 United States presidential election"), King endorsed [Gary Hart](/wiki/Gary_Hart "Gary Hart")\'s presidential campaign.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}153[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-153)^ During the [2008 presidential election](/wiki/2008_United_States_presidential_election "2008 United States presidential election"), King endorsed [Barack Obama](/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}154[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-154)^ In 2016, King was one of many writers who signed a letter condemning the candidacy of [Donald Trump](/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}155[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-155)^ In the [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries"), King endorsed [Elizabeth Warren](/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren")\'s [campaign](/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren_2020_presidential_campaign "Elizabeth Warren 2020 presidential campaign").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}156[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-156)^ Warren eventually suspended her campaign, and King later endorsed [Joe Biden](/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden")\'s [campaign](/wiki/Joe_Biden_2020_presidential_campaign "Joe Biden 2020 presidential campaign") in the [2020 general election](/wiki/2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}157[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-157)^ In July 2024, he called on Joe Biden to step down from the presidential race.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}158[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-158)^ King went on to endorse [Kamala Harris](/wiki/Kamala_Harris "Kamala Harris").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}159[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-159)^

On April 30, 2012, King published an article in *[The Daily Beast](/wiki/The_Daily_Beast "The Daily Beast")* calling for rich Americans, including himself, to pay more taxes, citing it as \"a practical necessity and moral imperative that those who have received much should be obligated to pay \... in the same proportion\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}160[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-DailyBeast-160)^ King testified in an August 2022 case brought by the U.S. [Justice Department](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") to block a \$2.2 billion merger of [Penguin Random House](/wiki/Penguin_Random_House "Penguin Random House") and [Simon & Schuster](/wiki/Simon_%26_Schuster "Simon & Schuster") (two of the \"Big Five\" book publishers).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}161[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-161)^ *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")* credited King\'s high-profile testimony, which was against his own publisher, with helping to convince presiding judge [Florence Y. Pan](/wiki/Florence_Y._Pan "Florence Y. Pan") with ultimately blocking the merger.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}162[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-162)^

In April 2008, King spoke out against HB 1423, a bill pending in the [Massachusetts state legislature](/wiki/Massachusetts_state_legislature "Massachusetts state legislature"){.mw-redirect} that would restrict or ban the sale of [violent video games](/wiki/Video_game_controversies "Video game controversies") to anyone under the age of 18. King argued that such laws allow legislators to ignore the economic divide between the rich and poor and the easy availability of guns, which he believed were the actual causes of violence.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}163[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-163)^ In 2013 King published an essay titled *[Guns](/wiki/Guns_(essay) "Guns (essay)"),* which discusses the [gun debate](/wiki/Gun_politics_in_the_United_States "Gun politics in the United States") in the wake of the [Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting](/wiki/Sandy_Hook_Elementary_School_shooting "Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting"). King called for gun owners to support a ban on automatic and semi-automatic weapons.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}164[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-164)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}165[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-165)^

In June 2018, King called for the release of the Ukrainian filmmaker [Oleg Sentsov](/wiki/Oleg_Sentsov "Oleg Sentsov"){.mw-redirect}, who was jailed in Russia.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}166[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-166)^ In July 2022, Stephen King appeared in a video call with the Russian pranksters [Vovan and Lexus](/wiki/Vovan_and_Lexus "Vovan and Lexus") who played the role of [Volodymyr Zelenskyy](/wiki/Volodymyr_Zelenskyy "Volodymyr Zelenskyy"). In the call Stephen King said \"You can always find things about people to pull them down. [Washington](/wiki/George_Washington "George Washington") and [Jefferson](/wiki/Thomas_Jefferson "Thomas Jefferson") were slave owners---that doesn\'t mean they didn\'t do many good things to the United States of America. There are always people who have flaws, we are humans. On the whole, I think [Bandera](/wiki/Stepan_Bandera "Stepan Bandera") is a great man, and you\'re a great man, and Viva Ukraine!\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}167[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-167)^ However, King later realized that he was pranked and apologized on Twitter, noting that he was not the only victim and \"other victims who fell for these guys include [J. K. Rowling](/wiki/J._K._Rowling "J. K. Rowling"), [Prince Harry](/wiki/Prince_Harry "Prince Harry"){.mw-redirect}, and [Justin Trudeau](/wiki/Justin_Trudeau "Justin Trudeau")\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}168[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-168)^

### Maine politics {#Maine_politics}

King endorsed [Shenna Bellows](/wiki/Shenna_Bellows "Shenna Bellows") in the [2014 U.S. Senate election](/wiki/2014_United_States_Senate_election_in_Maine "2014 United States Senate election in Maine") for the seat held by [Republican](/wiki/Maine_Republican_Party "Maine Republican Party") [Susan Collins](/wiki/Susan_Collins_(politician) "Susan Collins (politician)"){.mw-redirect}.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}169[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-169)^ King publicly criticized [Paul LePage](/wiki/Paul_LePage "Paul LePage") during LePage\'s tenure as [Governor of Maine](/wiki/Governor_of_Maine "Governor of Maine"), referring to him as one of [The Three Stooges](/wiki/The_Three_Stooges "The Three Stooges") (with then-[Florida Governor](/wiki/Governor_of_Florida "Governor of Florida") [Rick Scott](/wiki/Rick_Scott "Rick Scott") and then-[Wisconsin Governor](/wiki/Governor_of_Wisconsin "Governor of Wisconsin") [Scott Walker](/wiki/Scott_Walker_(politician) "Scott Walker (politician)") being the other two).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}170[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-stooges-170)^ He was critical of LePage for incorrectly suggesting in a 2015 radio address that King avoided paying Maine income taxes by living out of state for part of the year. The statement was later corrected by the governor\'s office, but no apology was issued. King said LePage was \"full of the stuff that makes the grass grow green\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}171[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-171)^ and demanded that LePage \"man up and apologize\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}172[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-172)^ LePage declined to apologize to King, stating, \"I never said Stephen King did not pay income taxes. What I said was, Stephen King\'s not in Maine right now. That\'s what I said.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}173[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-173)^

The attention garnered by the LePage criticism led to efforts to encourage King to run for Governor of Maine in the then-upcoming [2018 gubernatorial election](/wiki/2018_Maine_gubernatorial_election "2018 Maine gubernatorial election").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}174[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-174)^ King said he would not run or serve.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}175[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-kingno-175)^ King sent a tweet on June 30, 2015, calling LePage \"a terrible embarrassment to the state I live in and love. If he won\'t govern, he should resign.\" He later clarified that he was not calling on LePage to resign, but to \"go to work or go back home\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}176[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-176)^ On August 27, 2016, King called LePage \"a bigot, a homophobe, and a racist\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}177[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-177)^

## Philanthropy {#Philanthropy}

King subsidizes the [National Poetry Foundation](/wiki/National_Poetry_Foundation "National Poetry Foundation"), which was directed by his professor and mentor [Burton Hatlen](/wiki/Burton_Hatlen "Burton Hatlen"), and has endowed scholarships named for another professor, Edward Holmes. Mark Singer also notes Bangor\'s \"most monumental testament to King\'s philanthropy\", the \"Shawn T. Mansfield Baseball Complex, dedicated six years ago in memory of the son of a Little League coach and friend of King\'s who died at fourteen of cerebral palsy.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}22[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:Singer-22)^ King has stated that he donates approximately \$4 million per year \"to libraries, local fire departments that need updated lifesaving equipment ([Jaws of Life](/wiki/Jaws_of_Life "Jaws of Life"){.mw-redirect} tools are always a popular request), schools, and a scattering of organizations that underwrite the arts\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}160[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-DailyBeast-160)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}178[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-GuardianTax-178)^ The Stephen and Tabitha King Foundation, chaired by King and his wife, ranks sixth among Maine charities in terms of average annual giving, with over \$2.8 million in grants per year, according to [The Grantsmanship Center](/wiki/The_Grantsmanship_Center "The Grantsmanship Center").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}179[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-Grantsmanship-179)^

In 2002, King, [Peter Straub](/wiki/Peter_Straub "Peter Straub"), [John Grisham](/wiki/John_Grisham "John Grisham") and [Pat Conroy](/wiki/Pat_Conroy "Pat Conroy") organized the Wavedancer Benefit, a public reading to raise funds for the actor and audiobook reader [Frank Muller](/wiki/Frank_Muller "Frank Muller"), who had been injured in a motorcycle accident.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}180[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-180)^ Their reading was released as an audiobook.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}181[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-181)^ In November 2011, the STK Foundation donated \$70,000 in matched funding via his radio station to help pay the heating bills for families in need in his hometown of Bangor, Maine, during the winter.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}182[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-182)^ In February 2021, King\'s Foundation donated \$6,500 to help children from the Farwell Elementary School in [Lewiston, Maine](/wiki/Lewiston,_Maine "Lewiston, Maine"), to publish two novels on which they had been working over the course of several prior years, before being stopped due to the [COVID-19 pandemic in Maine](/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_Maine "COVID-19 pandemic in Maine").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}183[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-183)^

## Personal life {#Personal_life}

<figure typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Stephenking_house.JPG" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Stephenking_house.JPG/330px-Stephenking_house.JPG" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="768" data-file-width="1024" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6c/Stephenking_house.JPG/960px-Stephenking_house.JPG 2x" width="300" height="225" /></a>
<figcaption>King's home in <a href="/wiki/Bangor,_Maine" title="Bangor, Maine">Bangor</a></figcaption>
</figure>

After meeting her while studying at the [University of Maine](/wiki/University_of_Maine "University of Maine"),^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}184[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:0-184)^ King married [Tabitha Spruce](/wiki/Tabitha_King "Tabitha King") on January 2, 1971.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}185[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-185)^ She is also a novelist and philanthropist. She has been supportive of him throughout his career, even rescuing his early manuscript of *Carrie* from the trash when he doubted himself.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}184[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:0-184)^ They own and divide their time between three houses: one in [Bangor, Maine](/wiki/Bangor,_Maine "Bangor, Maine"), one in [Lovell, Maine](/wiki/Lovell,_Maine "Lovell, Maine"), and for the winter a waterfront mansion located off the [Gulf of Mexico](/wiki/Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") in [Sarasota, Florida](/wiki/Sarasota,_Florida "Sarasota, Florida"). King\'s home in Bangor has been described as an unofficial tourist attraction, and as of 2019^[\[update\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephen_King&action=edit){.external .text mw-original-href="//en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephen_King&action=edit"}^, the couple plan to convert it into a facility housing his archives and a writers\' retreat.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}186[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-186)^

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:Portrait_photograph_of_Owen_and_Stephen_King_by_James_Leonard,_c._1982.jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Portrait_photograph_of_Owen_and_Stephen_King_by_James_Leonard%2C_c._1982.jpg/250px-Portrait_photograph_of_Owen_and_Stephen_King_by_James_Leonard%2C_c._1982.jpg" class="mw-file-element mw-file-upright" style="--mw-file-upright: 0.75" data-file-height="1188" data-file-width="1027" decoding="async" srcset="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f2/Portrait_photograph_of_Owen_and_Stephen_King_by_James_Leonard%2C_c._1982.jpg/500px-Portrait_photograph_of_Owen_and_Stephen_King_by_James_Leonard%2C_c._1982.jpg 2x" width="190" height="220" /></a>
<figcaption>Portrait of <a href="/wiki/Owen_King" title="Owen King">Owen</a> and Stephen from the first edition of <em><a href="/wiki/Different_Seasons" title="Different Seasons">Different Seasons</a></em> (1982)</figcaption>
</figure>

The Kings have three children---two sons and a daughter, Naomi (born June 1, 1970), who is a [Unitarian Universalist Church](/wiki/Unitarian_Universalism "Unitarian Universalism") minister in [Plantation, Florida](/wiki/Plantation,_Florida "Plantation, Florida"), with her partner, [Thandeka](/wiki/Thandeka_(minister) "Thandeka (minister)").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}187[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-187)^ Both of King\'s sons are also professional authors: [Owen King](/wiki/Owen_King "Owen King") (born February 21, 1977)^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}184[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:0-184)^ published his first collection of stories, *We\'re All in This Together: A Novella and Stories*, in 2005. [Joseph Hillström King](/wiki/Joe_Hill_(writer) "Joe Hill (writer)") (born June 4, 1972),^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}184[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:0-184)^ who writes as Joe Hill, published his first collection of short stories, *[20th Century Ghosts](/wiki/20th_Century_Ghosts "20th Century Ghosts")*, in 2005.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}188[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-188)^

<figure class="mw-default-size" typeof="mw:File/Thumb">
<a href="/wiki/File:SA%26Mlr_(cropped)_(2).jpg" class="mw-file-description"><img src="//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/4/42/SA%26Mlr_%28cropped%29_%282%29.jpg" class="mw-file-element" data-file-height="330" data-file-width="210" decoding="async" width="210" height="330" /></a>
<figcaption>King wearing a <a href="/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox" title="Boston Red Sox">Boston Red Sox</a> jersey at a book signing in November 2004</figcaption>
</figure>

King is a longtime fan of baseball, particularly the [Boston Red Sox](/wiki/Boston_Red_Sox "Boston Red Sox"). In 1990, King published an essay about Owen\'s [Little League](/wiki/Little_League_Baseball "Little League Baseball") team in *[The New Yorker](/wiki/The_New_Yorker "The New Yorker")*.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}189[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-189)^ King and [Stewart O\'Nan](/wiki/Stewart_O%27Nan "Stewart O'Nan") coauthored *[Faithful](/wiki/Faithful_(book) "Faithful (book)")*, a chronicle of their correspondence about the historic [2004 Boston Red Sox season](/wiki/2004_Boston_Red_Sox_season "2004 Boston Red Sox season") which culminated in the Sox winning the [2004 World Series](/wiki/2004_World_Series "2004 World Series").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}190[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-190)^ The game features in King\'s novellas *[The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon](/wiki/The_Girl_Who_Loved_Tom_Gordon "The Girl Who Loved Tom Gordon")* (1999) and *[Blockade Billy](/wiki/Blockade_Billy "Blockade Billy")* (2010).

Music, particularly rock, plays a role in much of King\'s work. On the [BBC](/wiki/BBC "BBC") program *[Desert Island Discs](/wiki/Desert_Island_Discs "Desert Island Discs")*, King\'s number one choice was [Bob Dylan](/wiki/Bob_Dylan "Bob Dylan")\'s \"[Desolation Row](/wiki/Desolation_Row "Desolation Row")\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}191[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-191)^ On another BBC program, *Paperback Writers*, he made new selections, among them [AC/DC](/wiki/AC/DC "AC/DC")\'s [\"Stiff Upper Lip\"](/wiki/Stiff_Upper_Lip_(AC/DC_song) "Stiff Upper Lip (AC/DC song)"), [Danny & the Juniors](/wiki/Danny_%26_the_Juniors "Danny & the Juniors")\'s \"[At the Hop](/wiki/At_the_Hop "At the Hop")\" and [Creedence Clearwater Revival](/wiki/Creedence_Clearwater_Revival "Creedence Clearwater Revival")\'s \"[It Came Out of the Sky](/wiki/It_Came_Out_of_the_Sky "It Came Out of the Sky")\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}192[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-192)^ He played guitar for the [Rock Bottom Remainders](/wiki/Rock_Bottom_Remainders "Rock Bottom Remainders"), a [charity supergroup](/wiki/Charity_supergroup "Charity supergroup") whose members included [Amy Tan](/wiki/Amy_Tan "Amy Tan"), [Barbara Kingsolver](/wiki/Barbara_Kingsolver "Barbara Kingsolver"), [Dave Barry](/wiki/Dave_Barry "Dave Barry"), [Scott Turow](/wiki/Scott_Turow "Scott Turow"), [James McBride](/wiki/James_McBride_(writer) "James McBride (writer)"), [Mitch Albom](/wiki/Mitch_Albom "Mitch Albom"), [Roy Blount, Jr.](/wiki/Roy_Blount,_Jr. "Roy Blount, Jr."){.mw-redirect}, [Matt Groening](/wiki/Matt_Groening "Matt Groening"), [Greg Iles](/wiki/Greg_Iles "Greg Iles"), [Kathi Kamen Goldmark](/wiki/Kathi_Kamen_Goldmark "Kathi Kamen Goldmark") and other authors. They released an album, *[Stranger Than Fiction](/wiki/Stranger_than_Fiction_(compilation_album) "Stranger than Fiction (compilation album)")* (1998), under Goldmark\'s label, Don\'t Quit Your Day Job Records.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}193[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-193)^ King and his band-mates coauthored *Midlife Confidential: The Rock Bottom Remainders Tour America With Three Chords and an Attitude* (1994) and the e-book *Hard Listening: The Greatest Rock Band Ever (of Authors) Tells All* (2013).^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}194[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-194)^ King\'s favorite books about music are [Greil Marcus](/wiki/Greil_Marcus "Greil Marcus")\'s *[Mystery Train](/wiki/Mystery_Train_(book) "Mystery Train (book)")* and *[Lipstick Traces](/wiki/Lipstick_Traces:_A_Secret_History_of_the_20th_Century "Lipstick Traces: A Secret History of the 20th Century")* and Chris Willman\'s *Rednecks and Bluenecks*.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}18[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:ByTheBook-18)^

King and his wife own the Zone Corporation, a radio station group established in 1983 to acquire WACZ in Bangor, which was renamed [WZON](/wiki/WZON "WZON").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}195[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-bdn-zonestart-195)[[\[]{.cite-bracket}196[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-196)^ Two additional stations, [WKIT-FM](/wiki/WKIT-FM "WKIT-FM"){.mw-redirect} and [WNSW](/wiki/WNSW_(Maine) "WNSW (Maine)") in [Brewer](/wiki/Brewer,_Maine "Brewer, Maine"), were added in 1995;^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}197[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-bdn-wkitwnswbuy-197)^ WNSW was quickly closed down.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}198[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-bdn-wnswclosure-198)^ A third station, WDME-FM in [Dover-Foxcroft](/wiki/Dover-Foxcroft,_Maine "Dover-Foxcroft, Maine") (later renamed [WZLO](/wiki/WZLO "WZLO")), was acquired in 2001.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}199[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-bdn-saletozone-199)^ In December 2024, King announced that the stations would shut down at the end of the year. He cited his advancing age and financial losses from the stations as reasons for the closure.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}200[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-200)^ Ahead of the planned closure, King reached a deal to sell WKIT to two Bangor businessmen; WZON and WZLO remain slated for closure.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}201[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-wabi-wkitsale-201)^

King remains a voracious reader. In [J. Peder Zane](/wiki/John_Peder_Zane "John Peder Zane")\'s *The Top Ten: Authors Pick Their Favorite Books*, King chose *[The Golden Argosy](/wiki/The_Golden_Argosy_(book) "The Golden Argosy (book)")*, *[Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](/wiki/Adventures_of_Huckleberry_Finn "Adventures of Huckleberry Finn")*, *[The Satanic Verses](/wiki/The_Satanic_Verses "The Satanic Verses")*, *[McTeague](/wiki/McTeague "McTeague")*, *[Lord of the Flies](/wiki/Lord_of_the_Flies "Lord of the Flies")*, *[Bleak House](/wiki/Bleak_House "Bleak House")*, *[Nineteen Eighty-Four](/wiki/Nineteen_Eighty-Four "Nineteen Eighty-Four")*, *[The Raj Quartet](/wiki/The_Raj_Quartet "The Raj Quartet")*, *[Light in August](/wiki/Light_in_August "Light in August")* and *[Blood Meridian](/wiki/Blood_Meridian "Blood Meridian")*. In 2022, he provided another list of ten favorite books; *Lord of the Flies*, *Nineteen Eighty-Four* and *Blood Meridian* remained, and he added [*Ship of Fools*](/wiki/Ship_of_Fools_(Porter_novel) "Ship of Fools (Porter novel)"), *[The Orphan Master\'s Son](/wiki/The_Orphan_Master%27s_Son "The Orphan Master's Son")*, *[Invisible Man](/wiki/Invisible_Man "Invisible Man")*, *[Watership Down](/wiki/Watership_Down "Watership Down")*, *[The Hair of Harold Roux](/wiki/The_Hair_of_Harold_Roux "The Hair of Harold Roux")*, *[American Pastoral](/wiki/American_Pastoral "American Pastoral")* and *[The Lord of the Rings](/wiki/The_Lord_of_the_Rings "The Lord of the Rings")*. He added, \"Although [Anthony Powell](/wiki/Anthony_Powell "Anthony Powell")\'s novels should probably be on here, especially the sublimely titled *[Casanova\'s Chinese Restaurant](/wiki/Casanova%27s_Chinese_Restaurant "Casanova's Chinese Restaurant")* and *[Books Do Furnish a Room](/wiki/Books_Do_Furnish_a_Room "Books Do Furnish a Room")*. And [Paul Scott](/wiki/Paul_Scott_(novelist) "Paul Scott (novelist)")\'s Raj Quartet. And at least six novels by [Patricia Highsmith](/wiki/Patricia_Highsmith "Patricia Highsmith"). And what about [Patrick O\'Brian](/wiki/Patrick_O%27Brian "Patrick O'Brian")? See how hard this is to do?\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}202[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-202)\[*[[better source needed]{title="This claim needs references to better sources. (April 2026)"}](/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")*\]^

When asked about his reading habits, King replied, \"I\'m sort of an omnivore, apt to go from the latest [John Sandford](/wiki/John_Sandford_(novelist) "John Sandford (novelist)") to [D. H. Lawrence](/wiki/D._H._Lawrence "D. H. Lawrence") to [Cormac McCarthy](/wiki/Cormac_McCarthy "Cormac McCarthy").\" When asked what books we\'d be surprised to find on his shelves, he answered \"Poetry, maybe? I love [Anne Sexton](/wiki/Anne_Sexton "Anne Sexton"), [Richard Wilbur](/wiki/Richard_Wilbur "Richard Wilbur"), [W. B. Yeats](/wiki/W._B._Yeats "W. B. Yeats"). The poetry I come back to again and again are the narrative poems of [Stephen Dobyns](/wiki/Stephen_Dobyns "Stephen Dobyns").\" When asked which novel he comes back to, he named [Thomas Williams](/wiki/Thomas_Williams_(writer) "Thomas Williams (writer)")\'s *The Hair of Harold Roux.* When asked who his favorite novelist is, he said \"Probably [Don Robertson](/wiki/Don_Robertson_(author) "Don Robertson (author)"), author of *Paradise Falls*, *The Ideal, Genuine Man* and the marvelously titled *Miss Margaret Ridpath and the Dismantling of the Universe.* What I appreciate most in novels and novelists is generosity, a complete baring of the heart and mind, and Robertson always did that. He also wrote the best single line I\'ve ever read in a novel: Of a funeral he wrote, \'There were that day, o Lord, squadrons of birds.\'\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}18[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:ByTheBook-18)^

### []{#Car_accident_and_thoughts_of_retirement .anchor}Car accident and aftermath {#Car_accident_and_aftermath}

On June 19, 1999, at about 4:30 pm, King was walking on the shoulder of [Maine State Route 5](/wiki/Maine_State_Route_5 "Maine State Route 5"), in [Lovell, Maine](/wiki/Lovell,_Maine "Lovell, Maine"). Driver Bryan Edwin Smith, distracted by an unrestrained dog moving in the back of his minivan, struck King, who landed in a depression in the ground about 14 feet (four meters) from the pavement of Route 5.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}203[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-UKOnWriting-203)[: 206 ]{title="Page / location: 206"}^ Early reports at the time from Oxford County Sheriff deputy Matt Baker claimed King was hit from behind, and some witnesses said the driver was not speeding, reckless, or drinking.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}204[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-204)^

Smith was later arrested and charged with [driving to endanger](/wiki/Reckless_driving#Maine "Reckless driving") and aggravated assault. He pleaded guilty to the lesser charge of driving to endanger and was sentenced to six months in county jail (suspended) and had his driving license suspended for a year.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}205[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-205)^ In his book *On Writing*, King states he was heading north, walking against the traffic. Shortly before the crash took place, a woman in a car, also northbound, passed King first followed by a light blue Dodge van. The van was looping from one side of the road to the other, and the woman told her passenger she hoped \"that guy in the van doesn\'t hit him\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}203[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-UKOnWriting-203)[: 206 ]{title="Page / location: 206"}^

King was conscious enough to give the deputy phone numbers to contact his family but was in considerable pain. He was transported to Northern Cumberland Hospital in Bridgton and then flown by air ambulance to [Central Maine Medical Center](/wiki/Central_Maine_Medical_Center "Central Maine Medical Center") (CMMC) in [Lewiston](/wiki/Lewiston,_Maine "Lewiston, Maine"). His injuries---a collapsed right lung, multiple fractures of his right leg, scalp laceration and a broken hip---kept him at CMMC until July 9. His leg bones were so shattered that doctors initially considered amputating his leg but stabilized the bones in the leg with an [external fixator](/wiki/External_fixator "External fixator"){.mw-redirect}.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}206[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-206)^ After five operations in 10 days and physical therapy, King resumed work on *On Writing* in July, though his hip was still shattered and he could sit for only about 40 minutes before the pain became unbearable.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}203[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-UKOnWriting-203)[: 216 ]{title="Page / location: 216"}^

King\'s wife got in touch with his lawyer to purchase Smith\'s van, reportedly to prevent it from appearing on [eBay](/wiki/EBay "EBay"). He recalls: \"When I was in the hospital, mostly unconscious, my wife got a lawyer who\'s just a friend of the family\... And she got in touch with him and said, buy it so that somebody else doesn\'t buy it and decide to break it up and sell it on eBay, on the Internet. And so he did. And for about six months, I did have these, sort of, fantasies of smashing the van up. But my wife---I don\'t always listen to her the first time, but sooner or later, she usually gets through. And what she says makes more sense than what I had planned. And her thought was that the best thing to do would be to very quietly remove it from this plane of existence, which is what we did.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}54[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-:Craft-54)^

### Other media appearances {#Other_media_appearances}

In *[The Princess Bride](/wiki/The_Princess_Bride_(novel) "The Princess Bride (novel)")*, [William Goldman](/wiki/William_Goldman "William Goldman") writes that Stephen King is \"doing the abridgment\" of the fictional book *Buttercup\'s Baby.*^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}207[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-207)^ King explains this is an inside joke from Goldman, \"who\'s an old friend. He\'s done the screen adaptations for a number of my novels. He did [*Misery*](/wiki/Misery_(film) "Misery (film)"), *[Dreamcatcher](/wiki/Dreamcatcher_(2003_film) "Dreamcatcher (2003 film)")* and he also did [*Hearts in Atlantis*](/wiki/Hearts_in_Atlantis_(film) "Hearts in Atlantis (film)"), and although he\'s not credited, he worked on [*Dolores Claiborne*](/wiki/Dolores_Claiborne_(film) "Dolores Claiborne (film)") as well, so Bill and I go back a long way. I admired his books before I ever met him and as a kind of return tip of the cap, he put me in that book *The Princess Bride*.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}151[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-OfficialFAQ-151)^

In 1988, the band [Blue Öyster Cult](/wiki/Blue_%C3%96yster_Cult "Blue Öyster Cult") recorded an updated version of its 1974 song [\"Astronomy\"](/wiki/Astronomy_(song) "Astronomy (song)"); the single released for radio play featured a narrative intro spoken by King.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}208[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-BOC-208)^ In 2012, King provided the narration for [Shooter Jennings](/wiki/Shooter_Jennings "Shooter Jennings")\'s album *[Black Ribbons](/wiki/Black_Ribbons "Black Ribbons")*.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}209[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-209)^ King was a contestant on *[Celebrity Jeopardy!](/wiki/List_of_Jeopardy!_tournaments_and_events#Celebrity_Jeopardy!_and_variants "List of Jeopardy! tournaments and events")* in 1995 and 1998.^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}210[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-210)^ He has made cameos in adaptations of his work, and appeared as the character Bachman on *[Sons of Anarchy](/wiki/Sons_of_Anarchy "Sons of Anarchy")*; the name is a nod to his pseudonym [Richard Bachman](/wiki/Richard_Bachman "Richard Bachman").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}211[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-211)^ He voiced himself in *[The Simpsons](/wiki/The_Simpsons "The Simpsons")* episode \"[Insane Clown Poppy](/wiki/Insane_Clown_Poppy "Insane Clown Poppy")\", where he appears with fellow authors Amy Tan, [John Updike](/wiki/John_Updike "John Updike") and [Tom Wolfe](/wiki/Tom_Wolfe "Tom Wolfe") at a book fair. King tells [Marge](/wiki/Marge_Simpson "Marge Simpson") he is taking a break from horror to write a biography of [Benjamin Franklin](/wiki/Benjamin_Franklin "Benjamin Franklin").^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}212[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-212)^

*[Carrie](/wiki/Carrie_(novel) "Carrie (novel)")* was included on the [New York Public Library](/wiki/New_York_Public_Library "New York Public Library")\'s list of Books of the Century under the category \"Pop Culture Mass & Entertainment\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}236[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-236)^ In 2008, *On Writing* was ranked 21st on *[Entertainment Weekly](/wiki/Entertainment_Weekly "Entertainment Weekly")*[\']{.nowrap style="padding-left:0.1em;"}s list of \"The New Classics: The 100 Best Reads from 1983 to 2008\".^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}237[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-237)^ It also made [*Time*\'s](/wiki/Time_(magazine) "Time (magazine)") list of the 100 greatest nonfiction books published since the magazine\'s founding in 1923. Gilbert Cruz wrote, \"it\'s the most practical and unpretentious writer\'s manual around---as practical and unpretentious as its author, who, yes, just happens to be one of the world\'s most famous novelists.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}238[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-238)^

*[11/22/63](/wiki/11/22/63 "11/22/63")* (2011) was named one of the five best fiction books of the year in *[The New York Times](/wiki/The_New_York_Times "The New York Times")*: \"Throughout his career, King has explored fresh ways to blend the ordinary and the supernatural. His new novel imagines a time portal in a Maine diner that lets an English teacher go back to 1958 in an effort to stop Lee Harvey Oswald and---rewardingly for readers---also allows King to reflect on questions of memory, fate and free will as he richly evokes midcentury America. The past guards its secrets, this novel reminds us, and the horror behind the quotidian is time itself.\"^[[\[]{.cite-bracket}239[\]]{.cite-bracket}](#cite_note-239)^
